title: #broadway #westend #cynthiaerivo #acting #theatre
transcript: Should stage actors always have their lines memorized? There's a lot of controversy right now as Cynthia Erivo is doing a one woman version of Dracula in the West End, and some people have noticed she's using a teleprompter to deliver her lines. But while this might seem like a bit of a cheat or a cop out, there's actually a long history of stuff like this. First of all, it's worth noting that she is in early previews, and it's actually quite standard for actors to have some sort of safety net during that point in the process. I've seen some very experienced professional stage actors call for line in early previews. As in, someone on the stage management team with a script in their hand has to deliver their line over a microphone for everyone to hear. And let me tell you, that's a lot more disruptive to the show than someone glancing at a teleprompter for a second. But even if she used a *prompter* for the rest of the production, that's still not so unprecedented. Back in 2015, Alexis Soloski wrote this article for the Guardian about a bunch of stars using assistance to get their lines, including Bruce Willis in Misery. And you might say, “well, he's not a stage actor” “he was just getting a pass ‘cause he's a movie star.” But Soloski also mentions some beloved and very experienced stage actors doing the same thing, like Al Pacino in China Doll, James Earl Jones and Cecily Tyson using earpieces or teleprompters, and even Angela Lansbury’s Tony-winning performance in Blithe Spirit. And this quote from Lansbury here is actually really important, because a lot of people right now are saying, “well, if i'm paying all this money to see a star,” “I don't want them to need any help with their lines.” But Lansbury kinda turns it around and says, well, if you're paying all this money to see a star, don't you want us to get the lines as correctly as possible? And if, for whatever reason, it's unduly difficult, don't you want us to have all the support we need? And you might say, “okay,, but most of the actors you just named are on the older side,” “and Cynthia Erivo is not. So why does she get a pass?” And why do the actors in Encores productions get a pass for using their scripts on stage? Well, in every single example I just named, there is some sort of additional barrier at play and some theoretical trade off for that barrier. Whether you're getting to see a show in early previews or getting to see an actor play an unusual number of roles that requires them to learn a huge amount of text. Whether you get to see older legends of the stage returning in roles that they might not be able to play without assistance, or with Encores, where the short rehearsal process is actually what enables these broadway stars to do material that might not get fully produced otherwise. Even with Bruce Willis, you might say, well, he's not a stage actor, he's just a movie star. And frankly, I saw the performance. It really wasn't very good. But of course, we now know that Bruce Willis has extremely severe dementia that's forced him to stop acting. And this was ten years ago? Who knows if he was experiencing some early symptoms of that back then? I don't know if he was, but that's kind of my point. People might have certain challenges that are maybe none of our business. And while his performance was admittedly bad, I don't necessarily think it was bad because he had to use a prompter. Just like you can have Angela Lansbury deliver a tony winning performance with an earpiece. Now, I haven't seen Cynthia Erivo in Dracula, so I can't speak to whether it meets the standard of quality that was sold to its audiences. But I think as you criticize it, it's important to ask yourself, “did her using a teleprompter” “actually detract from my experience as an audience member?” “or am I just being kind of sanctimonious?”
classificationReason: Commentary about the controversy of Cynthia Erivo using a teleprompter during her West End Dracula one-woman show. That production is not on the list, and the creator is discussing industry practice/news rather than reviewing a production they attended.
